title: Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency (streaming, presigned URLs, async metadata queue, reactive WebFlux, backpressure/rate limiting).
shortTitle: Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency

s1_definition.profdef: A large-file upload microservice accepts files of a hundred megabytes or more from many clients at once without exhausting server memory or threads. The key design moves are: never buffer the whole file in memory, instead stream it; prefer offloading the actual bytes to object storage directly from the client using presigned URLs so the application server handles only control-plane requests; process file metadata asynchronously through a message queue; use a reactive, non-blocking stack such as Spring WebFlux so a few threads serve thousands of concurrent uploads; and apply backpressure and rate limiting so a flood of uploads cannot overwhelm downstream systems.
s1_definition.analogy: Customers of National Bank of India need to upload large documents: scanned loan files, years of statements, KYC videos. Imagine the branch clerk trying to personally carry every customer's heavy suitcase into the vault. With one clerk and a thousand customers, the clerk collapses. Instead, the bank gives each customer a one-time pass (presigned URL) to drive their own suitcase straight to the warehouse (object storage) through a loading dock, while the clerk only writes down "Rajesh dropped off suitcase 7 at 3pm" on a slip and puts that slip in an in-tray (queue) for later filing. The clerk never lifts a suitcase, so one clerk serves thousands.
s1_definition.oneliner: Don't move big bytes through your server; mint a presigned URL so the client uploads straight to object storage, and handle only lightweight metadata asynchronously on a non-blocking stack.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A large-file upload microservice accepts files of a hundred megabytes or more from many clients at once without exhausting server memory or threads. The key design moves are: never buffer the whole file in memory, instead stream it; prefer offloading the actual bytes to object storage directly from the client using presigned URLs so the application server handles only control-plane requests; process file metadata asynchronously through a message queue; use a reactive, non-blocking stack such as Spring WebFlux so a few threads serve thousands of concurrent uploads; and apply backpressure and rate limiting so a flood of uploads cannot overwhelm downstream systems.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Customers of National Bank of India need to upload large documents: scanned loan files, years of statements, KYC videos. Imagine the branch clerk trying to personally carry every customer's heavy suitcase into the vault. With one clerk and a thousand customers, the clerk collapses. Instead, the bank gives each customer a one-time pass (presigned URL) to drive their own suitcase straight to the warehouse (object storage) through a loading dock, while the clerk only writes down "Rajesh dropped off suitcase 7 at 3pm" on a slip and puts that slip in an in-tray (queue) for later filing. The clerk never lifts a suitcase, so one clerk serves thousands.

**One line to remember:** Don't move big bytes through your server; mint a presigned URL so the client uploads straight to object storage, and handle only lightweight metadata asynchronously on a non-blocking stack.

sections.s2_technical:
The first principle is never buffer a large file in memory. A naive Spring MVC controller that takes a `MultipartFile` and calls `getBytes()` loads the entire file into the heap. A hundred concurrent 100 MB uploads is 10 GB of heap, which is an instant OutOfMemoryError. Even streaming the `InputStream` through your server still consumes a thread and network bandwidth for the whole duration of each upload, so under high concurrency the thread pool saturates.

The better architecture is to keep the bytes off your server entirely using presigned URLs. Object storage such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage can issue a short-lived, cryptographically signed URL that grants permission to upload one specific object for a few minutes. The flow is: the client calls your API `POST /api/v1/uploads` with just the filename and size; your service validates and returns a presigned URL; the client uploads the raw bytes directly to S3 using that URL; S3 stores the object; your service never touches the file content. Your API only handles tiny JSON control requests, so one small instance serves enormous upload volume.

For files in the multi-gigabyte range, a single presigned PUT is not enough, so you use S3 multipart upload: the client splits the file into parts (say 10 MB each), requests a presigned URL per part, uploads parts in parallel, and finally calls a complete step that stitches them together. This also gives resumability: a failed part is retried without re-uploading the whole file.

Metadata is processed asynchronously. When the upload finishes, you record metadata: who uploaded, filename, size, checksum, storage key. You do not do heavy work (virus scan, thumbnail, indexing) inline on the upload request. Instead you drop an event onto a message queue such as Kafka or SQS, and background workers consume it. This decouples the fast upload path from slow processing, so a burst of uploads does not block on scanning.

When you must stream through your own service (for example because the client cannot talk to S3 directly, or you need to inspect bytes in flight), use a reactive, non-blocking stack. Spring WebFlux with `Flux<DataBuffer>` streams the body in chunks without loading it all into memory, and because it is non-blocking, a handful of event-loop threads can serve thousands of simultaneous slow uploads instead of tying up one blocking thread per upload. The `ReactiveHttpInputMessage` body is a `Flux` of buffers that you pipe straight to a reactive S3 client.

Backpressure is the reactive mechanism that stops a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer. If the client uploads faster than S3 can accept, the reactive pipeline signals "slow down" upstream rather than buffering unbounded data in memory. WebFlux and reactive S3 clients honour this automatically through the Reactive Streams `request(n)` protocol, so memory stays bounded even under pressure.

Rate limiting protects the system from abuse and overload. You cap how many uploads a single user or the whole system can start per minute, using a token bucket, so a misbehaving client or a traffic spike cannot exhaust storage bandwidth or cost. You also enforce a maximum file size before issuing a presigned URL, so nobody can request a URL for a 50 GB file.

Validation and security matter. You validate the declared content type and, after upload, the actual MIME type from magic bytes rather than trusting the extension, enforce size limits, and scan untrusted content for viruses in the async pipeline before the file is marked usable. Presigned URLs are short-lived and scoped to one object and one operation, so a leaked URL expires quickly.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India lets customers upload large documents for loan applications: Rajesh (SAV2001) uploads a 150 MB scanned property file for a home loan, and thousands of other customers upload simultaneously during a festive loan campaign.

Problem 1 — the server ran out of memory. The first version took a MultipartFile and read all bytes into the heap. During the campaign, a few hundred concurrent 150 MB uploads blew the heap and crashed the service. This is why we must never buffer the whole file: we hand the client a presigned URL and let it upload directly to object storage.

Problem 2 — the upload thread pool saturated. Even after switching to streaming, every slow upload held a blocking thread for minutes, so a few hundred slow mobile uploads exhausted the thread pool and new customers got rejected. This is why we use a reactive non-blocking stack: a few event-loop threads serve thousands of slow uploads.

Problem 3 — virus scanning blocked every upload. The first design scanned the file inline before responding, so each upload waited thirty seconds for the scanner. This is why we process metadata and scanning asynchronously through a queue: the upload finishes fast, and a background worker scans and marks the file usable afterward.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the control plane: an `UploadService` that validates a request and issues a presigned URL (simulated), an idempotent metadata record, an async `MetadataQueue` that workers consume for scanning, and a `RateLimiter` using a token bucket. It processes Rajesh's 150 MB request and shows a rejected oversized request and a rate-limited request.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the control-plane demo
java -cp target/file-upload-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.upload.UploadDemo

# Run as a WebFlux service
java -jar target/file-upload-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# 1) Ask for a presigned URL
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/uploads \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"userId":"SAV2001","filename":"property_deed.pdf","sizeBytes":157286400,"declaredType":"application/pdf"}'

# 2) Client uploads bytes DIRECTLY to S3 using the returned URL (server not involved)
curl -X PUT "https://nbi-loan-documents.s3.amazonaws.com/SAV2001/....?X-Amz-Signature=..." \
  --upload-file property_deed.pdf
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh requests to upload a 150 MB PDF; Priya requests a 500 MB video; Rajesh fires 12 quick 1 MB requests.

Step 1: Rajesh's 150 MB request hits `requestUpload`. The rate limiter grants a token. The size 150 MB is under the 200 MB cap, so it passes.

Step 2: The service asks PresignService for a presigned PUT URL. It gets back a storage key like SAV2001/uuid/property_deed.pdf and a URL valid for five minutes. No file bytes have moved yet.

Step 3: The service records FileMetadata with status UPLOADING and publishes it to the metadata queue, then returns the ticket. The whole API call is tiny and fast.

Step 4: The client (not the server) uploads the 150 MB bytes directly to S3 using the presigned URL. Our service never touches those bytes, so memory and threads are untouched.

Step 5: The background ScanWorker polls the queue, picks up Rajesh's metadata, simulates a virus scan and magic-byte MIME verification, and sets status to SCANNED_CLEAN. This happens off the upload path, so the upload was never blocked by scanning.

Step 6: Priya's 500 MB request hits the size check and throws FileTooLargeException before any URL is issued. No storage, no bandwidth wasted.

Step 7: Rajesh's 12 rapid requests consume his 10 tokens; requests 11 and 12 throw RateLimitedException, protecting the system from a single user flooding it.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] TICKET for Rajesh: key=SAV2001/8f3a.../property_deed.pdf url=https://nbi-loan-documents.s3.amazonaws.com/...
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [SEVERE ] Priya oversized rejected: size 524288000 exceeds max 209715200
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [WARNING] Rate limited request #10: too many uploads for SAV2001
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [WARNING] Rate limited request #11: too many uploads for SAV2001
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] SCANNED SAV2001/8f3a.../property_deed.pdf (property_deed.pdf) → SCANNED_CLEAN
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To design a microservice for large file uploads under high concurrency, my guiding principle is that big bytes should never flow through my application server. A naive controller that reads a MultipartFile into memory will throw OutOfMemoryError the moment a few hundred clients upload hundred-megabyte files at once, and even streaming through my service still ties up a thread and bandwidth per upload, so the thread pool saturates. The architecture I reach for is presigned URLs: the client calls my API with just the filename, size, and type; I validate it and return a short-lived, signed URL scoped to one object; the client then uploads the raw bytes directly to object storage such as S3; and my service never touches the content. That way one small instance handles enormous upload volume, because it only serves tiny control-plane JSON requests.

For multi-gigabyte files I use S3 multipart upload, where the client splits the file into parts, gets a presigned URL per part, uploads them in parallel, and calls a complete step to stitch them together, which also gives resumability so a failed part is retried without re-uploading the whole file. I process all the heavy work asynchronously: when the upload finishes I record metadata and drop an event on a queue like Kafka, and a background worker fleet does virus scanning, MIME magic-byte verification, and thumbnailing. This decouples the fast upload path from slow processing, which is exactly the fix for the problem where inline scanning made every upload wait thirty seconds.

When I genuinely must stream bytes through my own service, for example to inspect them in flight, I use a reactive non-blocking stack like Spring WebFlux, where the body arrives as a Flux of data buffers that I pipe straight to a reactive storage client without ever holding the whole file in memory. Because the stack is non-blocking, a handful of event-loop threads serve thousands of simultaneous slow uploads instead of one blocking thread each, which solves the thread-pool saturation we hit on mobile. Reactive Streams backpressure keeps memory bounded: if the client uploads faster than storage can accept, the pipeline signals upstream to slow down rather than buffering unbounded data.

On my project at National Bank of India, customers like Rajesh upload 150-megabyte scanned property files during loan campaigns, thousands at once. We moved to presigned direct-to-S3 uploads so the server stopped running out of memory, processed metadata and scanning through a queue so uploads finished fast, and put the control plane on WebFlux so a few threads handled the concurrency. We enforce a maximum file size before issuing any URL so nobody can request a URL for a 50-gigabyte file, and a per-user token-bucket rate limit so one client cannot flood storage bandwidth or cost. We validate the real MIME type from magic bytes after upload rather than trusting the extension, and we scan untrusted content before marking a file usable, moving infected files to quarantine.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I keep the bytes off my server by minting short-lived presigned URLs so clients upload straight to object storage, I use multipart upload for very large files, I handle only lightweight metadata on a non-blocking WebFlux stack with backpressure, I push scanning and processing onto an async queue of background workers, and I guard the whole thing with size limits and per-user rate limiting so high concurrency never exhausts memory, threads, or cost.
